part-b: Mediterranean mooring step by step · Ocean Way
Stern-to mooring is how most Mediterranean harbours work. Here is how to prepare, approach and tie up with lazy lines or your own anchor, calmly and without drama.
Prepare fenders on both sides, two stern lines, a boathook and a briefed crew before you enter.
Learn your boat's prop walk and approach slowly astern, aiming upwind of the gap in a crosswind.
Walk the lazy line forward to the bow, or drop your anchor 3 to 4 boat lengths out and lay chain in a line.
Keep lines out of the water near the propeller.
In most Mediterranean harbours you do not lie alongside a pontoon. You moor
: the stern (back) of the boat is tied to the quay and the bow (front) is held off by a line or an anchor. It fits many boats into a small space and lets you step ashore over a passerelle (gangway).

Most marinas, and many town quays in Croatia and Greece, have heavy ground lines laid on the seabed. From each berth a thinner line, the lazy line, runs from the quay down to a mooring chain. You pick it up at the stern and take it to the bow.
On many town quays in the Greek islands and parts of Turkey there are no lazy lines. You drop your anchor well out from the quay and reverse in, laying chain as you go.
The approach is the same in both cases. Only what holds the bow differs.
Most mooring problems start with a crew that is not ready. Get everything set up well outside the harbour, in open water where you have time.
, at the widest part of the boat and near the stern. You may end up between two boats, and you will not always know which side gets the pressure.
, one each side, cleated on board, coiled and led outside everything so they can be thrown or handed ashore cleanly.
ready at the stern to pick up the lazy line.
(anchor winch) switched on and the anchor ready to drop, if you are using your own.
Who handles each stern line, who takes the lazy line or runs the windlass, who fends off. Agree simple hand signals, because the helm cannot hear the bow over the engine.
If there is a marinero (marina attendant), call the marina on VHF or by phone before you arrive. They will usually point you to a berth and hand you the lazy line.
Read the wind, the gap and your prop walk

Before you commit, stop off the berth and look. Where is the wind coming from, and how strong is it? Is the gap wide enough for your beam plus fenders? Are the neighbours' lines or anchor chains in the way?

. A propeller turning in reverse pushes the stern sideways as well as backwards. On most charter yachts with a right-handed propeller, the stern kicks to port (left) in astern. Check this for your boat in open water: put the engine in reverse with the wheel centred and watch which way the stern swings.

Use it. If the stern kicks to port, approach so that kick helps your final line-up, or start your turn early so the walk does not push you onto the boat next door. With a crosswind, approach from the upwind side and aim slightly upwind of the gap, because the bow will blow downwind the moment you slow down.
Here is the main sequence for a laid mooring, with the extra steps for your own anchor marked.
Line up some distance from the quay, stern towards the berth, and start going astern slowly. Get steerage (enough flow over the rudder to steer) before you reach the line of boats.

drop the anchor about 3 to 4 boat lengths out from the quay, in line with your berth. Let chain out steadily as you reverse so it lies in a straight line on the seabed. Do not let it pile up, and do not brake it until you are nearly in.
Reverse slowly, using short bursts of power and neutral. Approach no faster than you would be happy to hit the quay at.
About a metre off, stop the boat with a touch of forward. The crew steps or passes the windward (upwind) stern line ashore first, then the other.
pick it up with the boathook at the stern and hand it forward. Walk it along the side of the boat, outside the stanchions, to the bow.
Pull the lazy line in hand over hand until it is tight, then cleat it at the bow.
tension the chain with the windlass, gently, until it holds the bow and the anchor has bitten.
Adjust the stern lines so the stern is far enough off the quay that it cannot touch if the boat surges, but close enough to step ashore on the passerelle. Engine in neutral, then off.
Keep everything slow. A boat going astern at walking pace is easy to stop. One going at three knots is not.

A rope near the propeller can wrap it in seconds and stop the engine just when you need it. Keep stern lines out of the water. When you lift the lazy line, put the engine in neutral and walk it forward quickly so it sinks away from the stern. Never motor ahead hard while any line hangs over the stern.
When you use your own anchor, the most common problem is laying your chain across a neighbour's. When one of you leaves, the anchor comes up with the other boat's chain on it.

To avoid it, look at the angle of the neighbours' chains before you go in, drop your anchor straight out from your own berth rather than at an angle, and go in after boats either side of you have settled, if you can. If someone drops across your chain, tell them politely and early.

If you do lift someone else's chain, stop the windlass. Pass a line under their chain, make both ends fast on board, then lower your anchor a little so it drops free. Release one end of the line and let their chain fall back.

Brief the crew before you start. On a lazy line, rig the stern lines as slip lines (doubled back to the boat around the quay ring) so you can release them from on board. Let the lazy line go at the bow and wait until it has sunk well away. Then slip the stern lines and motor out gently ahead.

With your own anchor, slip the stern lines and bring in the chain with the windlass while the helm gives gentle ahead power to take the load off it. Keep the boat in line with the chain until the anchor is off the bottom.
Get the windward stern line ashore first. It stops the stern blowing downwind.
A little more speed gives more control. Do not crawl so slowly that the wind takes over the bow.
With your own anchor, drop a little upwind of your berth. The chain then holds the bow up as you reverse.
If it goes wrong, go out, reset and try again. There is no shame in a second approach.

On our courses you practise this in real harbours, with laid moorings and with your own anchor, until each crew member has done every role. You start in light wind and move on to crosswind berths once the routine feels calm.
Anchoring: choosing a spot, scope and holding · Ocean Way
A secure anchorage comes from three decisions: where you drop, how much chain you let out and whether the anchor has really set. This guide walks through each one.
Pick a bay sheltered from the forecast wind, with sand or mud and room to swing.
Let out at least 4 to 5 times the depth in chain, more if wind is coming.
Lower the anchor, lay chain while going astern, then set it under reverse power and check with a transit.
Rig a snubber, set an anchor alarm and, if you can, swim over the anchor to look.

A good night at anchor is decided before you lower anything. Start with the forecast, not with the view. Look at the wind expected overnight and tomorrow morning, then look for a bay that is open to anything else but closed to that direction.

Land should lie between you and the forecast wind. Watch for winds that change through the night. In the Aegean, a meltemi (the strong summer northerly) can blow hard into a bay that looked calm at lunchtime, and katabatic gusts can drop off high ground at night.

Sand and mud hold well. Weed, including the seagrass meadows common in the Mediterranean, holds poorly because the anchor slides over it. Rock gives no reliable hold and can trap the anchor. In some areas anchoring on seagrass is restricted, so check local rules.
Somewhere between about 4 and 12 metres suits most charter yachts. Too shallow and you may touch at low water or when the boat swings. Too deep and you will run out of chain.
You need a clear circle around your anchor at least as large as your chain length plus the length of the boat.
The chart and a good pilot book will show the bottom type and depths. Your eyes and the depth sounder (echo sounder) confirm them.
is the length of chain you let out compared with the depth. For all-chain rode (the line between anchor and boat), use
at least 4 to 5 times the depth

in settled weather, and more if wind is forecast. Measure depth from the bow roller, so add a metre or so to the sounder reading. Tidal range in most of the Mediterranean is small, but where it is larger, use the depth at high water.
In the table, depth means sounder depth plus the height of the bow roller.

Charter yachts typically carry 50 to 80 metres of chain, and it varies, so find out what you have before you leave the base. Chain is usually marked every 10 metres with paint or coloured tags. Learn the code on your boat.
Longer scope matters because the anchor holds best when the pull is horizontal. The weight of the chain lying on the seabed keeps the pull low and absorbs snatching as the boat moves.
Motor slowly into the bay and pick your spot, allowing for where the boat will lie once the chain is out.
Approach head to wind (bow pointing into the wind) and stop the boat over the spot.
the anchor to the bottom with the windlass. Do not let it drop in free fall. A heap of chain on top of the anchor can foul it.
As the boat drifts back or you go slowly astern, let out chain steadily so it lies in a line on the seabed rather than piling up.
When the planned scope is out, hold the chain and let the boat come up against it. You will feel the bow swing to face the anchor.
Set it under reverse power: build up gradually to a firm astern load and hold it for 20 to 30 seconds. If the boat keeps moving, the anchor is dragging. Lift it and try again.
Check that it is holding by taking a

: two fixed objects ashore that line up, such as a rock in front of a building, roughly abeam (at right angles to the boat). If they stay in line under reverse, you are not moving. A compass bearing on a fixed point works too. Recheck it after a while and whenever the wind gets up.
Once the anchor is set, rig a

: a length of stretchy rope hooked onto the chain and made fast on a bow cleat. Let out a little more chain so the snubber takes the load. It saves the windlass from strain and stops the chain jerking the boat. Catamarans use a
, a snubber with two arms led to each bow.

. Most chart plotters and many phone apps let you mark the anchor position and sound an alarm if the boat moves outside a set radius. Set the radius to about your chain length plus the boat length, so normal swinging does not trigger it.

Look at the boats around you. Yachts on chain swing differently from boats on rope, and catamarans move differently from monohulls. If you anchor too close, you may meet at 3 a.m. after a wind shift. By custom, the boat that arrived first has the stronger claim to its space, so if you are the newcomer, it is up to you to leave room.

In clear Mediterranean water, the best check of all is to look. Put on a mask and snorkel and swim over the anchor. You will see whether it has dug in, is lying on its side, or has caught on a patch of weed. A few minutes in the water can save a sleepless night.
Shore lines in Turkey and Greece

In many small bays on the Lycian coast, around Göcek, and in parts of Greece, there is no room to swing. Instead you drop the anchor and reverse towards the shore, then take a line from the stern to a rock, tree or ring ashore. Some bays have bollards or rings fixed for this.
Drop the anchor well out, as for Mediterranean mooring, so there is plenty of chain when you stop.
One crew member takes the shore line ashore by dinghy or swims with it. Lead it round the tree or rock and back to the boat, so you can release it from on board.
Protect trees with a sleeve or a strop. Do not tie to anything that could pull loose.
Think about the wind direction. A shore line works best with the wind blowing off the land. If wind is forecast from the side, use two shore lines, or choose another bay.

To lift the anchor, one crew member works the windlass and signals to the helm. Motor gently towards the chain so the windlass is not dragging the boat. Point the direction of the chain with an arm. When the chain is straight up and down, the anchor should break out. Raise it slowly, rinse off mud before it comes aboard, and make it fast before you speed up.
Never drive over your own chain, and keep fingers and feet clear of the windlass while it runs.

On our courses you practise this in different bays every day, choosing the spot, working out the scope and setting the anchor under power. You also take shore lines in narrow coves and swim over the anchor to see how well it has set.
Reading the weather: Beaufort, forecasts, meltemi · Ocean Way
Good skippers decide most of their day before they leave the berth. Here is how to read the Beaufort scale and a forecast, know the Mediterranean's local winds, and make a calm go or no-go call.
Forecast wind is the mean; plan and reef for the gusts.
Use several sources: national services, NAVTEX, VHF and grib apps.
The meltemi builds through the day, so sail early.
If in doubt, wait in harbour.

The Beaufort scale describes wind strength in "forces" from 0 to 12. Forecasts in Greece, Turkey and Croatia often give wind in Beaufort, while apps usually show knots (nautical miles per hour). You need to switch between the two without thinking.

The table covers the range a charter skipper meets in a normal season. The knots are the mean (average) wind, not the gusts. The last column is a rough guide for a typical 40-foot (12-metre) cruising yacht with a sensible crew. Your own limits depend on the boat, the crew and the sea.
Large wavelets, a few white crests
Good sailing; heeling, ready to reef
Moderate waves, many white horses, some spray
Large waves, foam crests everywhere, spray
Sea heaps up, foam blown in streaks
Deep reefs; stay in harbour if you can
Moderately high waves, spray blown off crests

The sea state for a given force also depends on fetch (the distance the wind has blown over open water) and on how long it has been blowing. A Force 6 in a sheltered bay is a very different thing from a Force 6 after two days across the open Aegean.
Use more than one source and compare them. If they disagree, plan for the stronger one.

The Hellenic National Meteorological Service (Greece), the Turkish State Meteorological Service and the Croatian Meteorological and Hydrological Service all publish marine forecasts by sea area, usually with English versions. These are the official forecasts, and they carry the gale warnings.

A small receiver on board that prints or displays safety messages, including weather forecasts and gale warnings, from coastal stations. The international service on 518 kHz is in English. You select the stations for your area.

Coast radio stations announce weather broadcasts on channel 16, then read them on a working channel. In Croatia there are continuous recorded forecasts on dedicated VHF channels. The pilot book (the sailing guide for the area) lists the channels and times.

A GRIB file is raw output from a computer weather model, shown as arrows or colours on a map. Apps are quick and visual, and you can compare several models. But models smooth out local effects, so they often under-read the wind near capes, in channels and below high land.
Wind is always named after the direction it comes

. A north wind blows from the north towards the south. On most apps the arrow flies with the wind, so it points to where the wind is going. Some apps use wind barbs instead: the shaft points into the wind, and each long feather is 10 knots, each short one 5 knots.

The headline wind speed is the mean wind, averaged over about ten minutes. Gusts are short bursts above that. In the Mediterranean summer, gusts are often a third to a half stronger than the mean, and more in the lee of high islands. A forecast of "18 knots, gusts 28" means you should rig the boat for 28.
Look at the trend through the day, not just one number. Check the time the wind is expected to build and the time it should ease, and plan your passage around them.

The meltemi is the summer wind of the Aegean. It blows from roughly May to September, strongest and most regular in July and August. It comes from the north-east in the north Aegean, from the north in the Cyclades, and turns north-west towards the Dodecanese and the south-west coast of Turkey.

It often starts light in the morning, builds towards midday and peaks in the afternoon. It may ease in the evening, but in a strong spell it can blow Force 6–7 day and night for several days. It comes with clear blue skies, so there are no clouds to warn you. Experienced Aegean skippers sail early, before it fills in, and choose routes that keep the wind behind the beam (off the side or from behind).

The sirocco is a warm south to south-east wind from North Africa. By the time it reaches Greece, Italy or Croatia it is humid and hazy, sometimes carrying reddish dust. In the Adriatic it is called the
. It usually builds over a day or more, and the long fetch raises a big, long swell. It is more common in spring and autumn.

in Croatian) is a cold north-east wind in the Adriatic that falls down the coastal mountains. It is very gusty and can arrive within minutes, sometimes from a clear sky. In the worst places, such as the Velebit Channel, gusts can exceed 50 knots. It is mostly a winter wind but can appear in summer. A cap of cloud sitting on the mountain tops is a classic warning sign. Croatian forecasts name the bora directly, so read them every morning.

Reefing means making the sails smaller. The old rule holds: the first time you wonder whether to reef, reef. A reef put in early is calm and easy. A reef put in late, with the boat over on her side and the crew tired, is how things break and people get hurt.
If the forecast is Force 5 or more, reef before you leave harbour. You can always shake it out.
Most charter yachts have a furling mainsail and a roller genoa (the large front sail). Ease the sheet to take the load off before you roll a sail in.
Reef for the gusts, not the mean wind.
Before rounding a cape or entering a channel, reduce sail first. Wind accelerates there.
Before each passage, the skipper makes a clear decision, and says it out loud to the crew. Work through these questions:
What is the mean wind and the gust forecast, and when does it peak?
Which direction is it from? Will you be beating (sailing towards the wind) or running with it?
Are there exposed stretches, capes or channels on the route?
Is the crew rested, experienced and not seasick? Is the boat in good order?
Is the destination sheltered from this wind? What is your plan B if conditions get worse?
Does your charter agreement set any wind limits?
If the honest answer to any of these worries you, wait. Waiting a day in harbour costs very little. Many good skippers simply leave at dawn and are tied up before the afternoon wind arrives.

High islands make their own gusts. In a meltemi, wind pours down the lee (sheltered) side of islands such as Andros, Tinos or Evia and hits the water in violent, shifting gusts, often much stronger than the forecast. The water close in may look calm. Watch for dark patches racing across the surface, reef before you get there, and give high headlands a wide berth.

On our courses you read the morning forecast from several sources, compare them and make the go or no-go call yourself. You practise reefing in harbour first, then under way as the wind builds, until it becomes routine.
Position fixing and dead reckoning for sailors · Ocean Way
A chartplotter tells you where you are until it doesn't. This guide covers the chart, dead reckoning, bearing fixes, transits and compass corrections, so you can always find your position on paper.
One minute of latitude is one nautical mile; measure on the side scale.
DR uses course and log distance; an EP adds leeway and current.
A small cocked hat means a good fix.
True, Variation, Magnetic, Deviation, Compass: add west, subtract east.
Every position on a chart is given by two numbers.
is how far north or south of the equator you are, from 0° to 90°.
is how far east or west of Greenwich, from 0° to 180°. Each degree is divided into 60 minutes. Most of the Mediterranean lies between about 30° and 46° North.

One minute of latitude equals one nautical mile (1,852 metres). So to measure distance, use the latitude scale on the left or right side of the chart, level with where you are measuring. Never use the longitude scale along the top and bottom: a minute of longitude gets shorter as you move away from the equator.

is the low-water level the printed depths are measured from. With very little tide in most of the Mediterranean, depths on the chart are close to what you will find. Also check the note on which horizontal datum the chart uses. Modern charts use WGS84, the same as GPS, but some older charts do not, and positions can then be offset.

A chartplotter is a superb tool, and you should use it. But it depends on power, a dry screen, a satellite signal and a chart that is correct. Any of these can fail. Batteries go flat. Some remote bays are charted from old surveys, and the electronic chart can be offset from reality. GPS signals can also be jammed or spoofed, and interference has been reported repeatedly in parts of the eastern Mediterranean in recent years.

A paper chart with your position marked every hour means that if the screen goes blank, you know where you are and where the dangers are. It is also the best way to understand what the plotter is telling you.
Dead reckoning (DR) is working out your position from where you were, which way you steered and how far you went. You need three things:
your last known position (a fix), with the time;
the course you steered, converted to true;
the distance run, from the log (the instrument that measures distance through the water).

Example: at 1000 you fixed your position off Hydra, the log read 12.4 and you steered 090°T. At 1100 the log reads 18.4, so you have run 6 miles. Draw a line from the fix along 090°, measure 6 miles on the latitude scale, and mark it with the time. That is your DR position.
A DR ignores everything that pushes the boat sideways. An estimated position (EP) adds it back. Mark it with a small triangle and the time.

is the sideways slip caused by the wind. Close-hauled (sailing as close to the wind as you can) in a fresh breeze, a cruising yacht may make 5–10° of leeway. With the wind behind, it is close to zero. Watch the angle between your wake and the centreline to judge it. Apply it away from the wind: if the wind is on the port (left) side, add leeway to your heading; on the starboard (right) side, subtract it.

Tidal streams are weak in most of the Mediterranean, but water still moves. Currents run through straits and channels, and a meltemi blowing for several days sets up a surface drift. They are often under a knot, but stronger in some places. Check the pilot book. If you know the set (direction) and rate, draw it from your water track for the time elapsed.
A fix is a position you have measured, not estimated. The classic method uses a hand-bearing compass, a small compass you hold to your eye.
Pick three objects that are on the chart and easy to identify: a lighthouse, a church, the end of a headland. They should be well spread, ideally 60° or more apart.
Take the bearings quickly. Take objects ahead or astern first and those on the beam (off the side) last, because beam bearings change fastest.
Note the time and the log reading.
Convert each bearing to true by applying variation.
Draw each line on the chart towards the object.
The three lines almost never meet at a point. They form a small triangle called the

. A small cocked hat means a good fix. A large one means a mistake: a wrongly identified object or a misread bearing. Take the bearings again. For safety, assume you are at the corner of the triangle nearest to danger.

is two charted objects in line, such as a beacon and a chapel. When they line up, you are exactly on the line through them. No compass is needed, so there is no compass error. Many harbours have leading marks or lights built for this. A transit is also a quick way to check your steering compass.

is a useful cross-check. If your fix puts you on the 20-metre contour but the echo sounder shows 45 metres, something is wrong. Know whether your sounder shows depth below the transducer, below the keel or below the surface.
Charts are drawn to true north. Your compass points to magnetic north, and it is also pulled aside by the boat's own metal and electrics. So you correct in two steps:

is the difference between true and magnetic north. It depends on place and year, and it is printed on the compass rose of the chart. In the Aegean it is small and east, around 5°E, and changing slowly.
is the error caused by the boat itself. It changes with the boat's heading and is shown on the boat's deviation card.
("True Virgins Make Dull Companions"). Going from true to compass, add west and subtract east.

Worked example: you want to steer 045°T. Variation is 5°E, so subtract: 040°M. The deviation card says 3°W on this heading, so add: 043°C. You steer 043 on the compass. Going the other way, from compass to true, you reverse the signs.
Metres, if the chart is right
Good near land; worse with distance

At sea, write up the log every hour, and at every change of course or sail. Record the time, log reading, course steered, speed, wind direction and force, barometer, and your position with how you got it (GPS, fix or EP). Note events too: reefing, engine on, sightings.
If everything electronic fails, your last log entry is the start point for a new DR. It is also the boat's official record of the passage.

On our courses you plot DR and EP on paper alongside the chartplotter, take three-point fixes along the coast and compare them with the GPS. Each hour you write up the log, so the routine stays with you after the course.
VHF radio: Mayday, Pan-Pan and everyday calls · Ocean Way
The VHF radio is your link to rescue services, marinas and other boats. Learn the channels, the phonetic alphabet and the exact words for Mayday, Pan-Pan, Sécurité and a routine marina call.
Channel 16 is for distress, safety and calling; talk on a working channel.
The red DSC button sends your MMSI and position automatically.
Mayday for grave and imminent danger, Pan-Pan for urgency.
You need an SRC to operate; the boat needs a ship station licence.
A marine VHF radio works by line of sight, so its range is usually 20–30 miles between ships and further to a coast station with a tall aerial. It has many channels, but one matters most.
is for distress, urgency and safety calls, and for calling another station. Every vessel with a VHF should listen to it at sea. You use it to make contact, then move to a working channel to talk.
Ship-to-ship chat goes on intership channels such as 6, 8, 72 or 77. Marinas and ports each have their own channel, listed in the pilot book.
carries digital DSC alerts only. You never speak on it.
This setting lets the radio listen to channel 16 and one other channel at the same time. It is useful in a marina approach, but keep 16 in the loop.
Use low power (1 watt) for nearby stations such as a marina, and high power (25 watts) for distance.
Letters sound alike over a crackling radio, so you spell words with the international phonetic alphabet. Say numbers digit by digit: "one five" for 15.

Most modern sets have DSC (Digital Selective Calling). Each boat has an MMSI (Maritime Mobile Service Identity), a nine-digit number programmed into the radio. When the radio is connected to the GPS, it knows the boat's position.

To send a distress alert, lift the cover over the red DISTRESS button and hold it down (usually for about five seconds) until the radio transmits. If there is time, first choose the nature of distress from the menu, such as fire or sinking. The alert carries your MMSI, position and time.
The alert goes out on channel 70 and the radio switches itself to channel 16.
The radio repeats the alert every few minutes until a station acknowledges it.
A coast station or rescue centre acknowledges by DSC.
You then make the Mayday voice call on channel 16 and keep listening.
to a vessel or a person, when you need immediate help: fire out of control, sinking, a person overboard you cannot recover. Speak slowly and clearly on channel 16, high power. The format:
THIS IS, followed by the boat name three times

"Mayday, Mayday, Mayday. This is sailing yacht Kalimera, Kalimera, Kalimera. Call sign Sierra Victor Alfa Two, MMSI two three nine one two three four five six. Mayday Kalimera. My position two miles south of Cape Sounion. Fire in the engine compartment, out of control. I require immediate assistance. Six persons on board. We are preparing to abandon to the liferaft. Over."
Then wait. If nobody answers, repeat the call. Give position as latitude and longitude from the GPS, or as a bearing and distance from a charted point.

Pan-Pan is the urgency call. Use it when the safety of the boat or a person is at risk, but the danger is not immediate: engine failure near a lee shore with time in hand, a serious injury, a broken rudder. The structure follows the Mayday, addressed to all stations.

"Pan-Pan, Pan-Pan, Pan-Pan. All stations, all stations, all stations. This is sailing yacht Kalimera, Kalimera, Kalimera. Call sign Sierra Victor Alfa Two, MMSI two three nine one two three four five six. My position two miles south of Kalymnos. Engine failure and torn mainsail, drifting slowly, no immediate danger. I require a tow. Four persons on board. Over."

Sécurité (say "say-cure-ee-tay") is the safety call, for navigation or weather warnings. Coast stations use it for gale warnings. You might use it to warn others of a floating container or an unlit buoy. Announce it on channel 16, "Sécurité, Sécurité, Sécurité, all stations, this is…", name the working channel, then switch there and give the message.
Most of your radio use is ordinary. To call a marina, set low power and the marina's working channel:
"Kos Marina, Kos Marina, this is sailing yacht Kalimera, Kalimera. Over."
When they answer, say what you need:
"Good afternoon. We are a 12-metre yacht, beam four metres, draft two metres, requesting a berth for two nights. We are 15 minutes away. Over."
They will give you a berth and often ask you to wait outside for a marinero (berthing assistant). Prepare lines and fenders while you wait.
I have finished; I expect a reply.
the conversation is finished. Never say "over and out".
I made a mistake; here is the right version.
silence. Used by the station controlling a distress. Stop transmitting on that channel until you hear

To operate a marine VHF with DSC you need an operator's certificate, normally the Short Range Certificate (SRC) or an equivalent. The boat also needs a ship station licence from its flag state, which lists its call sign and MMSI. Charter yachts are already licensed, but the operator's certificate is personal and is your responsibility.

Never test-transmit a Mayday, by voice or by pressing the red button. A false alert can launch a real rescue. Use your radio's DSC test call instead. If you send a distress alert by mistake, do not switch off. Cancel the alert on the radio, then call on channel 16: "All stations, all stations, all stations, this is (boat name ×3), MMSI…, position…, cancel my distress alert of (time). Over."

On our courses you practise every call on training radios first, until the formats come without notes. On passage you then handle the real everyday calls yourself, calling marinas and other boats on the working channels.
